questions.question: What is the first priority when a patient with suspected AF has hypotension and acute pulmonary edema?
choices: Complete an outpatient stroke-risk score first
Arrange emergency evaluation for hemodynamic instability
Schedule routine follow-up
Focus only on long-term exercise goals
questions.explanation: Hypotension and acute pulmonary edema can indicate instability; emergency assessment takes priority.

questions.question: Which statement about AF stroke prevention is most accurate?
choices: It is based only on whether AF is paroxysmal or persistent
It should be guided by validated thromboembolic risk assessment and reassessed over time
Successful rate control eliminates stroke risk
Aspirin always replaces anticoagulation
questions.explanation: Stroke-prevention decisions are based on thromboembolic risk, not AF pattern alone, and should be reassessed as clinical factors change.

questions.question: How should bleeding-risk assessment be used in AF care?
choices: As an automatic reason to withhold every anticoagulant
To identify and modify bleeding risks and support shared decision making
Only after a stroke occurs
Instead of reviewing medications and kidney function
questions.explanation: Bleeding review should identify modifiable risks and inform individualized decisions rather than function as an automatic exclusion.

questions.question: Which is a potential contributor to new or worsening AF?
choices: Hypertension, heart failure, thyroid disease, alcohol exposure, or infection
A recent normal fasting glucose result
A stable normal ECG
Correct medication access
questions.explanation: AF can be associated with cardiovascular disease, thyroid/pulmonary disease, alcohol, acute illness, and other modifiable or nonmodifiable contributors.

questions.question: Which three questions organize FNP AF management?
choices: Stability, symptom/rate-rhythm strategy, and stroke prevention
Only age, height, and weight
Only medication brand and cost
Only the last ECG date
questions.explanation: Safe AF care separates immediate stability, symptom/rate-rhythm management, and thromboembolic prevention.

questions.question: Why is aspirin not simply substituted for indicated anticoagulation in AF?
choices: It has no antiplatelet effect
It is not a recommended alternative for stroke reduction when anticoagulation is indicated and no separate antiplatelet indication exists
It controls rhythm better than cardioversion
It eliminates all bleeding risk
questions.explanation: Current guidance does not use aspirin as a substitute for indicated oral anticoagulation in this setting.

questions.question: What should be reviewed when considering an anticoagulation plan?
choices: Renal/hepatic function when relevant, interactions, dose, adherence, bleeding history, and access
Only the patient’s preferred pill color
Only the AF duration
Only a pulse reading
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation safety requires individualized dosing, interaction, organ-function, bleeding, adherence, and access review.

questions.question: When is cardiology or electrophysiology referral reasonable?
choices: Symptomatic recurrent AF, difficult control, heart failure, complex valve disease, or treatment complexity
Only when the patient has no symptoms
For a normal pulse only
Never after initial diagnosis
questions.explanation: Complex, recurrent, symptomatic, or structurally complicated AF often benefits from specialist collaboration.

questions.question: Which ongoing intervention supports AF outcomes?
choices: Optimize blood pressure and comorbidities while addressing sleep, alcohol, tobacco, weight, and access barriers
Avoid all follow-up after rhythm documentation
Treat anticoagulation as a one-time decision
Ignore medication cost
questions.explanation: Risk-factor modification and feasible longitudinal care are core components of AF management.

questions.question: What is the FNP-level AF principle?
choices: Treat an irregular pulse in isolation
Integrate stability, triggers, symptom strategy, stroke prevention, monitoring, and patient goals
Use one rate target for every person
Delay care until all symptoms resolve
questions.explanation: High-quality AF care is individualized, longitudinal, and safety-focused.
